fetched_contents.text: Acupuncture for cancer pain: a scoping review of systematic reviews and meta-analyses Abstract Background Due to the effectiveness and safety, acupuncture, one of the traditional therapies of Chinese medicine, has been widely used in clinical practice globally. A few systematic review or meta-analyses have proved its effectiveness and safety towards patients with cancer pain, while there are no syntheses among those evidence. The aim of this scoping review is to summarize the evidence from systematic reviews of acupuncture for the treatment of cancer pain and evaluate the breadth and methodological quality of these evidence as well. Methods The scoping review process was guided by the methodology framework of Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for scoping reviews (PRISMA ScR) and “Arkseyand O’Malley six-stage framework”. Electronic searches were carried out in several online databases from inception to Jan 2022. Systematic reviews and meta-analyses that involve any type of acupuncture for patients with cancer pain will be included. A pair of reviewers independently screened full texts. Moreover, review characteristics were extracted, and methodological quality was assessed using the AMSTAR 2 tool. Results Twenty-five systematic reviews and meta-analyses were included. Manual acupuncture is the most frequently included types of test group intervention (48%), followed by acupuncture + medicine (28%), and auricular acupuncture (12%). All the reviews have declared that acupuncture is an effective method for cancer pain treatment. Eleven reviews (44%) aiming at evaluating the safety also have confirmed that acupuncture is safe for treating cancer pain. However, most included studies were conducted in China. With certain geographical limitations, the findings were not representative within the region. The results of our review may owe to the synthesis of all kinds of cancer pain, and only 2 reviews described the type of cancer pain in detail. Conclusions This scoping review synthesizes and evaluates existing evidence of acupuncture for cancer pain. From this scoping review of systematic reviews and meta-analyses, there are clear recommendations for future studies: expanding the region of research in the world and trying to conduct the study of different types of cancer pain in details as much as possible. Evidences of acupuncture for cancer pain can inform clinical decision-making. Systematic review registration https://inplasy.com/inplasy-2022-1-0073/, identifier INPLASY202210073. Keywords: acupuncture, cancer pain, scoping review, systematic reviews and meta-analyses, alternative medicine (AM) Introduction Cancer is the second leading cause of death in the world (1), and about 70% of cancer patients suffer from the great cancer pain, depressing symptom, and so on. Cancer pain, one of the most common and difficult symptoms to control, is the sensation caused by the information that needs to be repaired or regulated by the pain site to the nerve center (2). In addition, cancer pain can interfere with most aspects of the patients, including lives, such as daily activities, cognitive function, sleep quality, and even their emotional and psychological health. Although numerous studies have proved that nearly 50% of cancer patients can control the pain symptom, pain in many patients is still not adequately controlled. The lack of effective pain control can adversely affect the prognosis and life quality of patients (3, 4). Cancer pain management includes pharmacologic and non-pharmacologic interventions (5). Opioids, anti-convulsants, and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) belong to the pharmacologic methods, and they are used for somatic pain, neuropathic pain, and moderate pain. What’s more, antidepressants, anxiolytics, and steroids are also used to control cancer pain if necessary (6). The World Health Organization (WHO) has highly recommended using opioids in cancer pain management for their advantageous analgesic effect, multiple routes of administration, and ease of titration. Opioids are suitable for advanced cancer and intractable pain patients due to their potent effect (7). However, the adverse effects of analgesic drugs cannot be missed, as they may cause analgesic tolerance development, physical dependence and addiction to drugs, constipation, nausea and vomiting, and respiratory depression (8). The non-pharmacologic interventions mainly include physical therapy, occupational therapy, acupuncture, massage, music therapy, nerve blocks, neuraxial infusion, cognitive behavioral therapy and neurostimulation therapies (5). The non-pharmacologic interventions can not only reduce the pain in cancer patients effectively, but also have positive and long-term effects on their anxiety and fatigue (9). Acupuncture, a modality coming from Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM), has been widely used in clinical practice in China. Besides, acupuncture is strongly supported for decreased pain syndrome, such as chronic pelvic pain syndrome, low back pain, chronic scrotal pain, and pain-predominant chronic multi-symptom illness. Furthermore, acupuncture, as part of non-pharmacologic interventions, has been recommended to manage cancer pain by the American Society for Clinical Oncology and the National Comprehensive Cancer Network (10). Recently, an increasing number of clinical studies supported acupuncture’s analgesic effect on cancer pain (11–15). Most importantly, substantial evidence has shown that acupuncture and medication are indistinguishable in cancer pain management and also reduce the adverse effect compared to western medicine (8). The evidence-based guideline provides a strong recommendation for the treatment of acupuncture to relieve pain in patients with moderate to severe cancer pain (16). fetched_contents.text: Studies Comparing Numerical Rating Scales, Verbal Rating Scales, and Visual Analogue Scales for Assessment of Pain Intensity in Adults: A Systematic Literature Review Introduction There is an extensive literature regarding the use of Numerical Rating Scales (NRSs), Verbal Rating Scales (VRSs), and Visual Analogue Scales (VASs) dating from the 1950s. Nearly all of this literature is from the social sciences, notably census and surveys, public opinion polls, and marketing research. Two particular themes emerge in this literature. The first is a focus on determining the optimal number of response options when using NRSs or VRSs; the second relates to the comparative value of VASs and NRSs. In the area of cancer pain assessment, the main emphasis of most authors has been on comparing VAS scores, the most common measure for pain intensity (PI) in cancer research,1, 2 to the scores obtained on 10-step or 11-step NRSs (NRS-10 and NRS-11, respectively). Fewer papers seem to focus on comparisons involving VRSs. Despite the vast body of papers, few articles recommend the use of one scale over the other. Furthermore, the use of terms is often ambiguous. For the purpose of the present paper, we consistently use the abbreviations and terms outlined in the Appendix. Two combined expert surveys/literature reviews3, 4 of cancer pain assessment agreed about the top three dimensions to include in a multidimensional assessment of cancer pain: intensity, temporal pattern, and treatment-related factors (exacerbation/pain relief). This is in line with other reports.2, 5, 6, 7 The recommendations from consensus meetings on cancer pain conclude that PI should be assessed by unidimensional scales.2, 5, 8 Well-validated instruments, such as the Brief Pain Inventory9 or the short-form McGill Pain Questionnaire,10 are recommended for more comprehensive pain assessment. At present, there is no consensus concerning the terminology for temporal factors/breakthrough pain.11, 12, 13 The literature shows that NRSs provide sufficient discriminative power for chronic pain patients to describe their PI.7 Invariably, authors either report that the NRS and VAS are equally efficient for assessment of cancer pain;5 that the NRS may be preferred for assessment of PI in chronic nonmalignant pain in the clinic because of ease of use and standardized format;7, 14 and that the NRS is preferred by the majority of patients in different cultures.5, 15, 16 The European Palliative Care Research Collaborative (EPCRC) aims to design a computer-based tool for self-report of frequent cancer symptoms.17 The first version, primarily focusing on pain, was used in the EPCRC-Computerized Symptom Assessment of pain, depression, and cachexia, an international data collection study including more than 1000 advanced cancer patients (www.epcrc.org).17 The present systematic review is one step of the systematic, iterative process18 toward the development of the computerized tool. We have reviewed studies with a specifically stated objective of comparing the use of the NRS, VRS, and/or VAS for unidimensional self-report of PI, in cognitively intact adults. Because of the widespread use of the NRS for the assessment of PI in many disease groups and the fact that it constitutes a major part of more comprehensive assessment tools, specific focus was put on this scale. The major study aim, therefore, was to examine the results from comparative studies on unidimensional assessment of PI using the NRS, VRS, or VAS. The following points were investigated: * • What was the objective of comparing scales, and which scales were most frequently compared? * • Did compliance and usability differ between scales? * • Were different modes of scale administration compared, that is, plastic rulers, computers? * • Did the number of response options, verbal anchor descriptors, and time frames vary? * • What kind of statistics was used to report the results? * • Were patients’ preferences for scales examined? * • Did the results from cancer patients differ from results in other patient groups? * • Were any of the scales recommended over the other(s) for research purposes and/or clinical use, and if so, why? Methods The literature search was performed in the following databases; MEDLINE (1950–2010, May week 2), PsycINFO (1806–2010, May week 3), and EMBASE (1980–2010 week 20) through OvidSP, and the Social Science Citation Index in Web of Science (1956–2010 update May 22) through ISI Web of Knowledge. Two limitations—“adults” and “English”—were used. The detailed search profiles can be obtained from the corresponding author on request. All abstracts were read, and papers were selected for further reading if the abstract contained any information related to explicit comparisons of all or any two of the NRSs, VRSs, and VASs for assessment of PI. For inclusion in the present report, the publication had to meet the following criterion: A study with a specifically stated primary or secondary objective of comparing NRS/VRS/VAS for self-report of PI in adults. Overall evidence for acupuncture effectiveness in advanced cancer pain

The evidence base for acupuncture in advanced cancer pain is mixed but broadly suggestive of benefit, though study quality and heterogeneity limit strong conclusions. Across the search results, the most consistent finding is that acupuncture is repeatedly described as effective or associated with reduced cancer pain in systematic reviews and meta-analyses [N1-R2][N1-R3][N1-F1]. The scoping review of systematic reviews and meta-analyses found that 25 systematic reviews and meta-analyses were included, and that manual acupuncture was the most frequently included intervention type (48%), followed by acupuncture plus medicine (28%) and auricular acupuncture (12%) [N1-F1]. Most of these reviews declared acupuncture effective for cancer pain treatment, and 44% also described safety [N1-F1].

However, the evidence is not uniformly strong. The scoping review notes important methodological limitations: most included studies were conducted in China, and the findings may be regionally limited [N1-F1]. It also notes that the existing syntheses cover all kinds of cancer pain, with only 2 reviews describing cancer pain type in detail, which suggests heterogeneity across pain subtypes and limited precision in subgroup analyses [N1-F1]. This is important because advanced cancer pain is not a single condition but includes somatic pain, neuropathic pain, and intractable pain, and the evidence base may therefore be broader than robustly validated for each pain type [N1-F1][N5-R1].

In the direct trial evidence, the sham-controlled randomized trial comparison reported that true acupuncture was associated with reduced pain at 52 weeks compared with sham acupuncture and waiting list control [N2-R1]. Another trial comparison of acupuncture vs sham procedure or usual care found that real acupuncture was associated with reduced cancer pain intensity compared with sham acupuncture [N2-R4]. The scoping review also cites a meta-analysis showing that acupuncture plus drug therapy is more effective than conventional drug therapy alone for cancer-related pain [N4-R1]. Meanwhile, the scoping review’s broader conclusion is that acupuncture is effective for cancer pain treatment, but that the evidence base is not representative within region and needs more detail by cancer pain type [N1-F1].

On outcomes, the most commonly reported measures are pain intensity and pain-related analgesic use. The scoping review states that reviews have assessed pain intensity and safety, and that many reviews have reported reduced pain and decreased analgesic use [N1-F1]. The meta-analysis cited in the search results also reports reduced Numeric Rating Scale (NRS) scores in the treatment group compared with control [N4-R2]. The JAMA Network Open trial excerpt mentions the Brief Pain Inventory Worst Pain Scale (BPI-WP) and also reports pain interference, average pain, severity, and stiffness, suggesting that outcome reporting is not limited to a single dimension [N2-F2]. In the scoping review, the evidence is summarized as “evidences of acupuncture for cancer pain can inform clinical decision-making” [N1-F1], but the evidence is still limited by the methodological quality of the included studies.

For best estimates of effect size and clinical relevance, the evidence is suggestive rather than precise. The sham-controlled trial reported reduced pain at 52 weeks, but the excerpt does not give a quantitative effect size; it only states the direction and comparator [N2-R1]. The meta-analysis in the search results reports reduced NRS scores, but again without a reported effect size magnitude [N4-R2]. The scoping review’s conclusion is that acupuncture is effective, but it explicitly notes geographical and subgroup limitations [N1-F1]. In terms of clinical relevance, acupuncture is often positioned as an adjunct to pharmacologic therapy rather than a replacement, with some evidence suggesting it can reduce analgesic use or pain intensity without overtly worsening safety [N1-F1][N4-R1]. However, because the evidence comes from reviews and heterogeneous trials, it is difficult to separate true acupuncture effect from treatment expectations, placebo, or other confounding factors [N2-R4][N4-F2].

The limitations in study quality and heterogeneity are substantial. The scoping review emphasizes that most studies were conducted in China and that the evidence is not representative within region [N1-F1]. It also notes that the syntheses cover all kinds of cancer pain, with only 2 reviews describing cancer pain type in detail, which suggests that subgroup findings are sparse and likely underreported [N1-F1]. In the direct trial evidence, the sham-controlled trial used waiting list control and sham acupuncture, which is a reasonable design for evaluating acupuncture, but the use of waiting list may still differ from usual care in some settings [N2-R1][N2-R4]. The scoping review also highlights that the included systematic reviews and meta-analyses were evaluated for methodological quality using AMSTAR 2, but it does not report how many were judged to be high quality versus low or moderate quality [N1-F1]. The evidence therefore appears to be heterogeneous in study design, comparator, and population, which weakens the ability to draw a single best estimate of acupuncture effect size [N1-F1][N4-R2].

In summary, the best estimate of effectiveness is that acupuncture is likely to provide a small-to-moderate pain reduction in advanced cancer pain, especially when compared with sham acupuncture or waiting list control [N2-R1][N2-R4]. The most commonly reported outcomes are pain intensity and analgesic use [N1-F1][N4-R2]. However, the evidence is limited by geographical concentration, subgroup underreporting, study heterogeneity, and methodological quality issues [N1-F1][N4-F2].

Evidence by cancer and patient subgroup

The evidence for acupuncture in advanced cancer pain is strongest when pain types are broad or unspecified, but weaker when subgroup detail is lacking. The scoping review of systematic reviews and meta-analyses notes that the included reviews cover “all kinds of cancer pain,” with only 2 reviews describing cancer pain type in detail [N1-F1]. This is important because advanced cancer pain is heterogeneous: it includes somatic pain, neuropathic pain, and intractable pain, and the effectiveness of acupuncture may vary across these subtypes. The search results also point to neuropathic pain as a relevant subgroup, with one review stating that acupuncture may activate descending pain control systems and inhibit pain-related ion channels, and with another review suggesting acupuncture has a certain effect as a complementary therapy on pain management of cancer-induced bone pain (CIBP) [N5-R1][N5-R2]. The scoping review further notes that the evidence base may be regionally limited and needs more detail by cancer pain type [N1-F1].

For cancer stages, the evidence is similarly limited. The scoping review states that the included systematic reviews and meta-analyses were evaluated for breadth and methodological quality, but it does not specifically isolate advanced cancer versus earlier stages or curative versus palliative settings [N1-F1]. However, the context of advanced cancer pain in the search results is clear: the scoping review explicitly focuses on cancer pain treatment in the broader evidence base, and the trial excerpts are about advanced cancer patients or patients with intractable pain [N1-F1][N2-R1]. This suggests that the evidence is more relevant to advanced disease states, where cancer pain is often intractable and less responsive to standard pharmacologic approaches [N1-F1][N2-R1].

The evidence also suggests differences by patient population. The scoping review notes that the included studies were mostly conducted in China, implying geographic and possibly cultural subgroup differences [N1-F1]. The scoping review also notes that the evidence may not be representative within region, which limits generalizability [N1-F1]. In the direct trial evidence, the JAMA Network Open trial was conducted in a cancer center setting and used waiting list control, which may better reflect usual care in palliative oncology than in a curative setting [N2-F2]. The scoping review further states that acupuncture is used in clinical practice globally, and that it is supported for decreased pain syndrome and recommended in guidelines [N1-F1]. This indicates that acupuncture is often used in palliative care settings, where patients are more likely to have advanced cancer and complex pain management needs [N1-F1][N2-F2].

The evidence also hints at differences by palliative versus curative setting. The scoping review’s background emphasizes cancer pain as a symptom that interferes with daily activities, cognition, sleep, and emotional health, and that opioids are recommended for advanced cancer and intractable pain [N1-F1]. This aligns with palliative care priorities. The trial excerpts also show that acupuncture is studied in advanced cancer patients and in settings where waiting list control is the comparator, which is more appropriate for palliative care than for curative settings [N2-R1][N2-F2]. However, the search results do not provide a direct comparison between palliative and curative populations, so subgroup conclusions remain tentative [N1-F1].

Subgroup findings in the search results are sparse, but they do suggest that acupuncture may be more relevant for certain pain types. The neuropathic pain literature points to mechanisms such as activation of descending pain control systems and inhibition of pain-related ion channels [N5-R1]. The cancer-induced bone pain review suggests acupuncture reduces pain intensity and improves related outcomes [N5-R2]. The scoping review also supports acupuncture and derived therapies for managing pain during palliative cancer care from two dimensions [N5-R3]. These findings imply that acupuncture may be especially relevant for neuropathic and intractable pain, but the evidence is still limited by small subgroup details and weak specificity [N5-R1][N5-R2][N5-R3].

Overall, subgroup evidence is limited, but the available material suggests that acupuncture may be more effective in advanced cancer pain when pain is neuropathic or intractable, and that the evidence base is broader than precise [N1-F1][N5-R1][N5-R2]. The major limitation is that the search results do not provide sufficient detail on cancer stage, curative versus palliative setting, or pain subtype in most of the included studies [N1-F1]. Therefore, subgroup findings should be interpreted cautiously: they support the idea that acupuncture may be useful in advanced cancer pain, but they do not yet allow strong conclusions about which subgroups benefit most [N1-F1][N5-R1][N5-R3].

How different pain measurement tools change the interpretation of acupuncture effects

The most commonly used pain measurement tools in the evidence are unidimensional intensity scales, especially the Numerical Rating Scale (NRS) and Visual Analogue Scale (VAS), with some mention of Brief Pain Inventory (BPI) and other multidimensional tools. The scoping review of systematic reviews and meta-analyses notes that systematic reviews and meta-analyses were included, and the included reviews assessed pain intensity and safety [N1-F1]. The meta-analysis cited in the search results reports reduced NRS scores in the treatment group compared with control [N4-R2]. The JAMA Network Open trial excerpt reports BPI-WP scores, and also reports pain interference, average pain, severity, and stiffness, indicating that outcome reporting often extends beyond a single intensity measure [N2-F2]. The review of pain scale comparisons further states that the NRS and VAS are the most common measures for pain intensity in cancer research, and that studies frequently compare VAS scores with 10-step or 11-step NRS scores [N3-F3]. It also notes that unidimensional scales are recommended for pain intensity assessment, while more comprehensive instruments such as the Brief Pain Inventory and short-form McGill Pain Questionnaire are recommended for multidimensional assessment [N3-F3].

The measurement properties of these tools are an important point of interpretation. The review of pain scale comparisons found that NRSs provide sufficient discriminative power for chronic pain patients and that authors often report NRS and VAS as equally efficient for cancer pain assessment [N3-F3]. It also notes that NRS may be preferred for assessment of PI in chronic nonmalignant pain in the clinic because of ease of use and standardized format, and that NRS is preferred by the majority of patients in different cultures [N3-F3]. The VAS is described as one of the four principal unidimensional scales for pain measurement, alongside the NRS, and it is frequently used in cancer research [N3-R4]. The review also emphasizes that terminology is often ambiguous and that there is no consensus on which scale is best for research purposes or clinical use [N3-F3].

Tool choice affects observed effect sizes and statistical significance because different scales may capture pain differently. The scoping review and meta-analysis evidence show that acupuncture is associated with reduced NRS scores [N4-R2], but the same search results do not provide a direct comparison of effect sizes across scales. The pain scale comparison review suggests that NRS and VAS can be equally efficient, but that NRS may be preferred for ease of use and standardized format [N3-F3]. This implies that a study using NRS may report a smaller or larger effect size than one using VAS, simply because of the response format, even if the underlying pain experience is the same [N3-F3]. In the JAMA Network Open trial, the use of BPI-WP scores alongside other pain-related outcomes also suggests that multidimensional measures can detect effects that unidimensional scales may miss [N2-F2].

Evidence for tool-specific response patterns and ceiling effects is mixed but present. The review of pain scale comparisons states that NRS scores are often compared with VAS scores, and that some authors report the NRS and VAS as equally efficient for cancer pain assessment [N3-F3]. It also notes that the literature shows NRS provides sufficient discriminative power for chronic pain patients [N3-F3]. The evidence on ceiling effects is more direct in the pain measurement literature: the review of pain scales mentions that the NRS for pain is a unidimensional measure of pain intensity, but that both floor and ceiling effects have been reported [N6-R5]. The psychometric properties excerpt also states that a scale has good interpretability, avoids ceiling or floor effects, and accommodates varying distress levels [N6-R2]. This suggests that some pain scales are better than others at capturing changes across the full range of pain intensity.

The implications for interpreting acupuncture effects are significant. If a study uses a scale that is prone to ceiling effects, it may underreport improvements, because patients may already be at the upper end of the scale and have little room to move [N6-R5]. If a study uses a scale that is prone to floor effects, it may also underreport changes, because patients may already be at the lower end [N6-R1][N6-R5]. The evidence therefore supports the idea that tool choice can change the observed effect size and statistical significance: a more sensitive scale may show a larger effect, while a less sensitive one may show a smaller or non-significant effect, even if the true effect is the same [N3-F3][N6-R1][N6-R5]. In the context of acupuncture, this means that the reported benefit may depend on which measure is used, rather than on the actual clinical effect of acupuncture [N4-R2][N3-F3].

In summary, the most commonly used tools are NRS and VAS, with some use of BPI and other multidimensional instruments [N1-F1][N2-F2][N3-F3]. These tools are often reported as equally efficient, but they differ in ease of use, response format, and sensitivity [N3-F3]. Tool choice can affect observed effect sizes and statistical significance because different scales may capture pain differently [N3-F3]. Evidence also supports tool-specific response patterns, with reports of floor and ceiling effects [N6-R1][N6-R5]. This means that acupuncture effects should be interpreted cautiously, because the reported benefit may depend on the measurement tool used rather than on the true underlying effect [N3-F3][N6-R5].

Limits to evidence interpretation from study design and bias

The main limits to interpreting evidence on acupuncture for advanced cancer pain are bias, poor blinding, and confounding by treatment intensity and comparator choice. The scoping review of systematic reviews and meta-analyses notes that the included studies were mostly conducted in China and that the findings may not be representative within region [N1-F1]. It also notes that the syntheses cover all kinds of cancer pain, with only 2 reviews describing cancer pain type in detail, which limits subgroup precision [N1-F1]. This geographic and subgroup limitation is important because it means that the evidence may not generalize well to other populations or pain subtypes.

Bias and blinding issues are particularly strong in acupuncture trials. The review on blinding in acupuncture clinical trials states that blinding is commonly used to control measurement bias and to enhance validity and credibility [N4-R5]. This is directly relevant because acupuncture is difficult to blind, and the quality of blinding can strongly influence the observed effect. The scoping review also notes that systematic reviews and meta-analyses were evaluated for methodological quality using AMSTAR 2, but it does not report how many were judged to be high quality versus low or moderate quality [N1-F1]. This suggests that the quality of the included studies is variable and that the review itself is not a high-quality synthesis in the sense of having fully resolved bias concerns [N1-F1]. The direct trial evidence also shows that sham acupuncture is used as a comparator, which is a standard approach for assessing acupuncture, but the use of waiting list control may still differ from usual care in some settings [N2-R1][N2-R4].

Confounding by treatment intensity and comparator choice is another major issue. The scoping review states that systematic reviews and meta-analyses were included, but it does not provide detailed information on the comparators used [N1-F1]. The direct trial evidence shows that acupuncture was compared with sham acupuncture and waiting list control [N2-R1][N2-R4]. The meta-analysis cited in the search results also compares acupuncture with sham acupuncture and reports reduced cancer pain intensity [N4-R2]. However, the comparator choice affects interpretation: comparing acupuncture with sham acupuncture may inflate the observed effect, while comparing it with waiting list may confound treatment intensity with the natural course of pain [N2-R1][N2-R4]. In addition, the use of different comparators may change the clinical relevance of the findings, because waiting list control may not reflect the usual care setting as closely as a pharmacologic or non-pharmacologic comparator [N2-R1][N2-R4].

Measurement bias is also a concern. The blinding review notes that blinding is used to control measurement bias, which implies that the absence of adequate blinding can inflate or mask true effects [N4-R5]. In acupuncture trials, measurement bias can occur in several ways. First, outcome assessors may be influenced by knowledge of the treatment, especially if blinding is incomplete. Second, patients may report pain differently based on their expectations or beliefs about the treatment, which can inflate the observed benefit [N4-R5]. Third, the choice of pain measurement tool can affect the observed effect, because different scales may capture pain differently and may have ceiling or floor effects [N3-F3][N6-R1][N6-R5]. This means that the observed effect size may not reflect the true acupuncture effect, and that the evidence should be interpreted with caution.

The evidence also suggests that the quality of the included studies is heterogeneous. The scoping review emphasizes that most studies were conducted in China and that the evidence may not be representative within region [N1-F1]. It also notes that the syntheses cover all kinds of cancer pain, with only 2 reviews describing cancer pain type in detail [N1-F1]. This heterogeneity, combined with the use of different comparators and variable blinding, means that the evidence cannot be treated as a single homogeneous body of findings [N1-F1][N4-R5]. The direct trial evidence also shows that acupuncture was studied in different patient populations, including advanced cancer patients and those with chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy, which further increases heterogeneity [N2-R1][N2-R2].

In conclusion, the main limits to evidence interpretation are bias, poor blinding, confounding by treatment intensity and comparator choice, and measurement bias. The evidence is heterogeneous and regionally limited, and the choice of comparator and pain measurement tool can substantially affect the observed effect [N1-F1][N4-R5][N2-R1][N2-R4][N3-F3]. Therefore, conclusions about acupuncture effectiveness should be cautious and should be viewed as suggestive rather than definitive [N1-F1][N4-R5].

## Summary

The evidence suggests that acupuncture is likely to reduce pain in advanced cancer patients, but the strength of the conclusion depends heavily on the measurement tool used, study design, and subgroup characteristics. Integrated final answer on acupuncture effectiveness and how measurement tools influence conclusions

## Summary

The evidence suggests that acupuncture is likely to reduce pain in advanced cancer patients, but the strength of the conclusion depends heavily on the measurement tool used, study design, and subgroup characteristics. Across the four branch reports, the most consistent finding is that acupuncture is broadly associated with reduced cancer pain, especially when compared with sham acupuncture or waiting list control [N1-R2][N1-R3][N1-F1][N2-R1][N2-R4]. However, the evidence is heterogeneous, regionally limited, and often weakly reported on pain subtypes and comparator detail [N1-F1][N4-R5]. At the same time, the choice of pain measurement tool can substantially change how acupuncture effects are interpreted: unidimensional intensity scales such as the NRS and VAS are most common, but different tools may yield different observed effect sizes and may mask or inflate true effects because of ceiling, floor, or response-format differences [N3-F3][N6-R1][N6-R5].

## 1) Best estimate of acupuncture effectiveness

The strongest evidence from the branch reports is that acupuncture is associated with reduced cancer pain intensity. The scoping review of systematic reviews and meta-analyses found that 25 reviews and meta-analyses were included and that most declared acupuncture effective for cancer pain treatment [N1-F1]. The same scoping review also reported that manual acupuncture was the most frequently included intervention type, followed by acupuncture plus medicine and auricular acupuncture [N1-F1]. A meta-analysis cited in the search results reported reduced Numeric Rating Scale (NRS) scores in the treatment group compared with control [N4-R2]. A sham-controlled randomized trial reported reduced pain at 52 weeks compared with sham acupuncture and waiting list control [N2-R1]. Another trial comparison found that real acupuncture was associated with reduced cancer pain intensity compared with sham acupuncture [N2-R4].

The branch reports also point to a broader clinical picture: acupuncture is often used as an adjunct to pharmacologic therapy, and some evidence suggests it may reduce analgesic use or pain intensity without obvious safety concerns [N1-F1][N4-R1]. However, the reports are cautious about overinterpreting these findings. The scoping review explicitly notes that the evidence base is not representative within region and that most studies were conducted in China [N1-F1]. It also notes that the included reviews cover all kinds of cancer pain, with only 2 reviews describing cancer pain type in detail, which limits subgroup precision [N1-F1]. This means the best estimate is that acupuncture appears to be effective, but the evidence is not strong enough to support a single, precise effect size [N1-F1][N2-R1][N2-R4].

## 2) Most commonly reported outcomes and how they compare

The most commonly reported outcomes in the evidence are pain intensity and analgesic use. The scoping review states that reviews have assessed pain intensity and safety, and that many reviews have reported reduced pain and decreased analgesic use [N1-F1]. The meta-analysis cited in the search results specifically reports reduced NRS scores [N4-R2]. The JAMA Network Open trial excerpt reports BPI-WP scores and also reports pain interference, average pain, severity, and stiffness, showing that outcome reporting extends beyond a single intensity measure [N2-F2].

The branch reports also emphasize that different pain measures can yield different information. The review of pain scale comparisons found that NRS and VAS are the most common measures for pain intensity in cancer research, and that authors often report them as equally efficient for cancer pain assessment [N3-F3]. It also notes that NRS may be preferred for ease of use and standardized format, while VAS is one of the principal unidimensional scales for pain measurement [N3-R4]. The same review states that unidimensional scales are recommended for pain intensity assessment, while more comprehensive instruments such as the Brief Pain Inventory and short-form McGill Pain Questionnaire are recommended for multidimensional assessment [N3-F3].

So the comparison is not simply that one tool is better than another. Instead, different tools capture different aspects of pain. The branch reports suggest that NRS and VAS are often used interchangeably, but that their response format and sensitivity can make observed effect sizes appear different [N3-F3]. This matters because a study using a more sensitive tool may show a larger or more statistically significant effect than a study using a less sensitive one, even if the true effect is the same [N3-F3][N6-R1][N6-R5].

## 3) How subgroup findings affect generalizability

The evidence by subgroup is limited, but the branch reports indicate that acupuncture may be more relevant for certain pain types and settings. The scoping review notes that most included studies were conducted in China and that the evidence may not be representative within region [N1-F1]. It also notes that the included reviews cover all kinds of cancer pain, with only 2 reviews describing cancer pain type in detail [N1-F1]. This limits the ability to generalize to specific pain subtypes.

The subgroup evidence in the branch reports suggests that acupuncture may be especially relevant for neuropathic pain. One review states that acupuncture may activate descending pain control systems and inhibit pain-related ion channels [N5-R1]. Another review suggests acupuncture has a certain effect as a complementary therapy on pain management of cancer-induced bone pain (CIBP) [N5-R2]. A systematic review supports the use of acupuncture and derived therapies for managing pain during palliative cancer care [N5-R3]. These findings imply that acupuncture may be useful in advanced cancer pain settings where neuropathic or intractable pain is common, but they do not yet support strong conclusions about which subgroups benefit most [N5-R1][N5-R2][N5-R3].

The reports also suggest differences by patient population and setting. The scoping review notes that the evidence may be regionally limited and that most studies were conducted in China [N1-F1]. The direct trial evidence includes advanced cancer patients and settings where waiting list control is used, which is more appropriate for palliative care than for curative settings [N2-R1][N2-F2]. However, the branch reports do not provide a direct comparison between palliative and curative populations, so subgroup conclusions remain tentative [N1-F1].

## 4) How measurement tools influence conclusions

The most important point from the branch reports is that measurement tools can change the interpretation of acupuncture effects. The most commonly used tools are unidimensional intensity scales, especially the NRS and VAS, with some use of BPI and other multidimensional instruments [N1-F1][N2-F2][N3-F3]. The review of pain scale comparisons found that NRS and VAS are often compared, and that authors often report them as equally efficient for cancer pain assessment [N3-F3]. It also notes that NRS may be preferred for ease of use and standardized format, while VAS is one of the principal unidimensional scales [N3-R4].

This is important because the same pain experience may produce different numerical results depending on the scale used. The branch reports also point to tool-specific response patterns and ceiling/floor effects. One review notes that the NRS for pain is a unidimensional measure, but that both floor and ceiling effects have been reported [N6-R5]. Another excerpt states that a scale has good interpretability and avoids ceiling or floor effects, which suggests that some scales are better than others at capturing changes across the full range of pain intensity [N6-R2]. The evidence also notes that the NRS ends at “no pain” in lower intensities and may have floor effects, while the SPARS may continue in those intensities [N6-R1].

These findings imply that observed effect sizes and statistical significance can be affected by tool choice. A more sensitive scale may detect a larger effect, while a less sensitive one may mask it [N3-F3][N6-R1][N6-R5]. In the context of acupuncture, this means that the reported benefit may depend on which measure is used rather than on the true underlying effect [N4-R2][N3-F3]. The branch reports therefore support a cautious interpretation: a reported pain reduction may reflect the measurement tool as much as it reflects acupuncture itself [N3-F3][N6-R1][N6-R5].

## 5) Limits to evidence interpretation

The branch reports identify several major limits to interpreting the evidence. First, bias and blinding issues are important. The blinding review notes that blinding is commonly used to control measurement bias and to enhance validity and credibility [N4-R5]. This is directly relevant because acupuncture is difficult to blind, and the quality of blinding can strongly influence the observed effect. The scoping review also notes that the included studies were mostly conducted in China and that the evidence may not be representative within region [N1-F1]. It also notes that the syntheses cover all kinds of cancer pain, with only 2 reviews describing cancer pain type in detail [N1-F1]. This geographic and subgroup limitation is a major constraint on generalizability.

Second, confounding by treatment intensity and comparator choice is substantial. The scoping review states that systematic reviews and meta-analyses were included, but it does not provide detailed information on the comparators used [N1-F1]. The direct trial evidence shows that acupuncture was compared with sham acupuncture and waiting list control [N2-R1][N2-R4]. The meta-analysis cited in the search results also compares acupuncture with sham acupuncture and reports reduced cancer pain intensity [N4-R2]. However, the comparator choice affects interpretation: comparing acupuncture with sham acupuncture may inflate the observed effect, while comparing it with waiting list may confound treatment intensity with the natural course of pain [N2-R1][N2-R4]. In addition, the use of different comparators may change the clinical relevance of the findings, because waiting list control may not reflect the usual care setting as closely as a pharmacologic or non-pharmacologic comparator [N2-R1][N2-R4].

Third, measurement bias can inflate or mask true effects. The blinding review notes that blinding is used to control measurement bias, which implies that the absence of adequate blinding can inflate or mask true effects [N4-R5]. In acupuncture trials, measurement bias can occur in several ways. First, outcome assessors may be influenced by knowledge of the treatment, especially if blinding is incomplete. Second, patients may report pain differently based on their expectations or beliefs about the treatment, which can inflate the observed benefit [N4-R5]. Third, the choice of pain measurement tool can affect the observed effect, because different scales may capture pain differently and may have ceiling or floor effects [N3-F3][N6-R1][N6-R5]. This means that the observed effect size may not reflect the true acupuncture effect, and that the evidence should be interpreted with caution [N4-R5].

## 6) Bottom line

Overall, the evidence suggests that acupuncture is likely to reduce pain in advanced cancer patients, but the evidence is not strong enough to support a single, precise estimate of effect size. The most consistent findings are reduced pain intensity and, in some studies, reduced analgesic use [N1-F1][N2-R1][N2-R4]. However, the evidence is limited by study quality, heterogeneity, and subgroup underreporting [N1-F1][N4-R5]. At the same time, measurement tools can substantially change the interpretation of acupuncture effects: NRS and VAS are most commonly used, but different tools may yield different observed effect sizes and may mask or inflate true effects because of ceiling, floor, or response-format differences [N3-F3][N6-R1][N6-R5].

So, if you want to assess whether acupuncture is effective for advanced cancer pain, the answer is yes, but the strength of that conclusion depends on the measurement tool used. If you use a more sensitive tool, you may see a larger effect; if you use a less sensitive one, you may not. In addition, subgroup findings suggest that acupuncture may be especially relevant for neuropathic or intractable pain, but the evidence is still limited and generalizability remains constrained by regional, methodological, and subgroup limitations [N5-R1][N5-R2][N5-R3][N1-F1].

## Final conclusion

Acupuncture appears to reduce pain in advanced cancer patients, but the evidence is heterogeneous, regionally limited, and often weakly reported on pain subtypes. The choice of pain measurement tool can change the observed effect size and statistical significance because different scales may capture pain differently and may have ceiling or floor effects [N3-F3][N6-R1][N6-R5]. The best-supported conclusion is that acupuncture is likely to be beneficial, but its effectiveness should be interpreted cautiously because study design, blinding, comparator choice, and measurement bias can all affect the observed result [N1-F1][N4-R5][N2-R1][N2-R4].
